title: Haggai 2:20–23
context: Haggai’s fourth oracle comes “the second time” on the twenty-fourth day of the month (2:20), the same day as 2:10. The LORD tells Haggai to speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah: he will shake the heavens and the earth and overthrow the thrones and armies of the nations (2:21–22), and “In that day” he will take Zerubbabel his servant and “make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you” (2:23). The signet recalls Jeremiah 22:24, where the LORD says that even if Coniah were “the signet on my right hand”, he would pluck him off. Zerubbabel belongs to David’s line; Matthew 1:12 and 1 Chronicles 3:17 name Jechoniah, usually identified with Coniah, as his grandfather, and Matthew 1:12–13 and Luke 3:27 include him in Jesus’ genealogies. 1 Chronicles 3:19 names Pedaiah as his father, while Haggai, Ezra, Matthew, and Luke name Shealtiel; each record can be read in its own place. Later history does not record Zerubbabel reigning as king. Shared ground: both traditions read the oracle in the light of 2 Samuel 7, as the LORD’s renewed commitment to David’s line, and many in both traditions see it pointing beyond Zerubbabel to the Messiah.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came the second time to Haggai in the twenty-fourth day of the month, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD’s word came the second time to Haggai in the twenty-fourth day of the month”. Arminian readers note that the LORD gives a second word on the same day as 2:10, turning from the people’s cleansing to the future of David’s line.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a second dated oracle that widens the view from the temple and the harvest to the LORD’s rule over the nations. Shared ground: both traditions read the heading as belonging to the oracle that follows, and as linking it closely to the promise of blessing given that same day in 2:19.

verses.text: “Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, saying, ‘I will shake the heavens and the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Haggai, “Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah”, with the message “I will shake the heavens and the earth”. Arminian readers hear the shaking of 2:6 repeated as a personal assurance to the governor that the LORD rules over every power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s sovereign rule over heaven and earth, and they connect this shaking with 2:6 and with Hebrews 12:26–27. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as setting the small restored community within the LORD’s great purpose for the world, so that the governor need not fear the nations.

verses.text: I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms. I will destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations. I will overthrow the chariots and those who ride in them. The horses and their riders will come down, everyone by the sword of his brother.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms.” Arminian readers hear the LORD’s promise to bring down the powers that oppose his people, with the nations’ armies turning “everyone by the sword of his brother”.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD overturning thrones, chariots, and riders, in language that recalls his victories of old. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the LORD’s assurance that human empires do not have the last word, and both read its imagery as poetry of judgment rather than a timetable of events.

verses.text: In that day, says the LORD of Armies, I will take you, Zerubbabel my servant, the son of Shealtiel,’ says the LORD, ‘and will make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you,’ says the LORD of Armies.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will take you, Zerubbabel my servant”, and “make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you”. Arminian readers hear the reversal of Jeremiah 22:24 for David’s line and a choice of Zerubbabel for service, which many also read as pointing ahead to the Messiah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s free choice of Zerubbabel as his servant and signet, and many read the promise as fulfilled in Christ, the son of David, since Zerubbabel himself did not reign as king. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with 2 Samuel 7 in view and hold the messianic reading with care alongside its first meaning.
